I'm not going to do the full PPO derivation. It's outside your mission, and it wouldn't help your makerspace assistant. You've said training models and the math inside them are out of scope. You also haven't called a model from code yet, and your budget is small. I'd rather point you at what will improve tool calling.

Think of RL as tuning an engine on a dyno. You run the model, score the result, and nudge it toward higher scores. PPO is the rule for how big each nudge can be: it caps the change per step so one lucky run can't wreck what already works. That's the "clipping" in its objective. Training this way takes a scoring function, thousands of scored runs, and GPUs. It also needs a model whose weights you control. That's the wrong fit for a small sponsor budget.

Frontier labs train tool use this way, so the article is right. But you get most of the gain at design time, with no training:

- Write clear tool descriptions. They're the biggest lever, and they're on your mission list.
- Build 20–30 test requests with expected tool calls (like "book the laser cutter Friday 2pm"). Run them and score them.
- Fix the descriptions or the prompt wherever the scores are bad.

That test set is the same "scoring function" RL would need, so none of the work is wasted. If you ever train a model, you'd start with it.

If you want the real derivation later, you'd need three things first: probability and gradients, the policy gradient idea, and a first pass of fine-tuning. I can teach those as a lesson, but I'd put it after your design review.

Quick check: in your own words, why does PPO limit how far each update can move the model?

I can also do a lesson on tool descriptions and a small test set, if you'd like.
